title: Apostolic Authority and Conduct
english: …weak brother, not eat in an idol's temple, so that he is not wounded. The one among you who thinks he knows something knows nothing, for he did not realize that others were being harmed by what these people knew.

On 1 Corinthians 8:6: He had said first, “There is no God but one” (1 Corinthians 8:4). So that he would not seem to cast the Son out of the Godhead, he added “the Father.” And truly there is no other Father but one; so too there is no other God the Son but one. If the Son is called the one Lord and the Father is no less Lord, then clearly, when the Father is called the one God, the Son is no less God. “From whom are all things” does not point to substance, since created things do not come from God's substance; the “from whom” points to the Father's will. Then, by saying “and we to him,” he lets us supply what the phrase leaves out: “but for us there is one God, and we hope in him.” Again, something is left out of “and we through him”: “we have been called,” or “we have been saved.” He is not saying that we came into being through him, for by saying “all things” he had already included “we.” “All things” means everything that came into being; “we” means those who were brought under his saving plan and are being saved.
What you gain is nothing; what harms the weaker ones is great.
On 1 Corinthians 8:10–12: What knowledge? That God is one and an idol is nothing in the world.

The second catena form adds: The one who does not have this knowledge, that God is one and an idol is nothing in the world, thinks he is eating idol food and is wounded. Your knowledge harms the weak one. Many even of those who have believed have not yet understood that there is no such thing as idol food, and they are harmed by the believer who eats.

On 1 Corinthians 8:13–9:1: I do not just say that I will not eat idol food; I will not eat meat at all if my brother is made to stumble by it. He shows that even where he had a right, such as being [fed] by them, he would not bear to burden anyone. He builds this case through many points. First he mentions his own rank, to show the grounds on which he could reasonably have received support had he wished to receive it, just as the others too received from those they received from. “I too,” he says, “am an apostle. I have authority over myself, and I am under no one who compels me to receive or forbids me. The other apostles may have something more than I do, in having been with Christ, but I am not without even that.”

On 1 Corinthians 9:2: To those who question me whether I am an apostle, this is my defense: you, my seal, and my teaching. Do I not give orders as an apostle? Do I not lay down laws for the churches? Am I under other teachers? So I have the right, but I do not use it to the full, so that I may not make some of little faith stumble because of me.
On 1 Corinthians 9:3: That is, the confirmation and the proof.
On 1 Corinthians 9:4: He shows that the law has laid down that those who serve, whether at altars or in the gospel, live from them.

On 1 Corinthians 9:5: By saying “wife” and adding “sister,” he made clear that the woman who travels with an apostle is fitting, chaste and pure, whether she was a spouse or not. Clearly women did travel with Peter and the others, eager for their teaching. He does not say this to cast blame, far from it. He is showing how far his own strictness of life went, and shaming the Corinthians into not living carelessly, so that they do not become a stumbling block to others.
On 1 Corinthians 9:6: Or are we alone forbidden to do what others do? He put in Barnabas as his fellow worker so as not to seem proud, as if he alone were doing right.
On 1 Corinthians 9:8: These are not my own words that I speak. Does not the law say the same?
On 1 Corinthians 9:15: “I have not written this,” he says, “to carry off something from you. Far from it!”
On 1 Corinthians 9:19: It is no great thing if you keep away from idol food for your brother's sake. I too made myself a slave to those I am not subject to, so that I might help many.

On 1 Corinthians 9:20: By “Jews” he means those who are Israelites by birth. By “those under the law” he means those who are not of their race but who keep the law of the Jews and have become proselytes.

On 1 Corinthians 9:21: By “those outside the law” he means the Greeks, who are not under the law of Moses. He did not say, “To the Greeks I became as a Greek,” because he would not stoop even to pretend to Greek religion. So by “those outside the law” he means those who have turned from the nations.

On 1 Corinthians 9:22: I seemed to those who came from the Greeks not to be under the law, and I bore that reputation in order to rescue them from Jewish observances. So he gave way to everyone at the start, bringing himself along with them, so that, having gone along with them, he might, little by little, toward himself…

added_allusions.reason: Quoted: οὐδεὶς θεὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix-b2): the old English was garbled and paraphrased. Retranslated every clause from the Greek. The opening finishes the second catena form's sentence on 8:1-3 begun in u04-open; of that form, "Even if we think we know something, we do not yet know anything" and "blessedness is to love God and be known by him, that is, to be made his own; for he is ignorant of no one, but is said not to know the ungodly" repeat the first form and are not printed again. On 8:10-12 the second form ("The one who does not have this knowledge ...") is printed as an addition except its last sentence ("what is gained by eating is not great, what harms the weaker is heavy"), which repeats the unlabeled sentence printed just before the 8:10-12 label. That unlabeled sentence has no verse label in the edition and stays unlabeled. The edition label "1 Kor 9," (no verse) is printed as 9:20, by the words (Jews, those under the law). γραφῆναι in the 9:1 note is read as τραφῆναι, [fed]. The 9:22 sentence runs on into u04-rem-mid, where its verb (ἐπισπάσηται, draw over) stands. Labels now one form.

title: Testing God and the End of the Age
english: …draw them over. People do not come to terms at all with those who agree with them in nothing, but they do with those who come part of the way to meet them.
On 1 Corinthians 9:23: Since the gospel too seems not to have made use of the law, I copied its way of managing things, handling matters as it wishes, so that in this very respect I may share in it.

On 1 Corinthians 9:24: He does not mean that one out of all of us is picked; otherwise people would have given up on themselves, seeing how hard success is. Clearly the picture is drawn with the nations he has just named in view. Everyone, he says, competes in this life as in a stadium: Jews by the law, Greeks by their error. But one alone is the word of truth, the one that wins and takes the prize. So run, so that you are not left behind with the rest.

On 1 Corinthians 9:25: What great thing is it, he says, if you abstain from meat for your brother's sake? The athlete must master himself in everything: in anger, in glory, and in all the rest. They do it to win a crown that perishes, but we a crown that does not. He did not say this idly. He was correcting those who, to fill their bellies, put on a show of philosophy and said that idol food is not idol food.

On 1 Corinthians 10:1–8: The inspired Paul brings forward the types from the old covenant and the shadows there that sketched in advance the truth to come, so as to sober the Corinthians by setting the ancients beside them. If, he says, those who were baptized into Moses, who was a type of Christ, in the cloud and the sea, who ate the manna, the spiritual food, and drank the spiritual drink from the rock, were struck down in the wilderness when they turned to drunkenness, fornication and idolatry, because they insulted the type and the shadow, what would those not suffer who sin against the truth itself?

On 1 Corinthians 10:9: Since they were saying, “For me there is no idol; I give thanks and eat,” this, he says, is putting the Lord to the test. When you do something Jesus did not command, as though you were trusting him, you are testing him rather than trusting him.

On 1 Corinthians 10:11: The coming of Christ has reached you, he says, and after it there will be no further commandment, no law, no prophets. By “the ends” he does not mean the last generation, at which the world will reach its completion, but the final way of life, the life in Christ, upon which the completion of the ages will arrive.
On 1 Corinthians 10:13: He did not pray that they should not be tested, since an untested man is unproven, but that they should be tested in a way they could bear.
The second catena form adds: From this he shows that those among them who believed had to endure some unpleasantness from their fellow citizens.
On 1 Corinthians 10:14: You see that everything he said before was being built up for this.
On 1 Corinthians 10:20: Do not look at their idols, which are nothing, but at the intent with which they sacrifice to demons and not to God. What is done there amounts to a denial of God.

On 1 Corinthians 10:22: It is written that God said to them through Moses, “They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god; they angered me with their idols” (Deuteronomy 32:21). The Corinthians were eating idol food. That is why he says, “Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?” meaning “Are we stirring him to anger?” “Are we stronger than he?” By this he showed that the Lord does not want us to eat idol food. So do not want, he says, what the Lord does not want, as though you were stronger and wiser than he.

On 1 Corinthians 10:25: It was likely that, in their scruples, they would no longer dare even to buy food at market for fear of hearing, “You bought idol food.” So he eases that fear. By “conscience” he means not the conscience of the one who knows that an idol is nothing, but that of the one who has seen someone buying the…

title: The Image of God and Order in the Assembly
english: …idol food, and who thinks that idol food is something.
On 1 Corinthians 10:26: What you eat belongs to the Lord, since the earth does too, and everything that fills it.
On 1 Corinthians 10:31: Do everything with care, so that people give glory to God because of you and do not stumble.

On 1 Corinthians 10:32: Do not become a cause of stumbling to Jews and Greeks: see that they do not flee the faith with your bad conduct as their excuse. Nor to the church of God: see that those of little faith are not made to stumble.
On 1 Corinthians 11:2: He praises them now, though they have gone wrong, so that from here on they may at least be persuaded by what he says.

On 1 Corinthians 11:3: He speaks to spur them on rather than to approve them, so that he can then make his exhortation firm in them: “But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.” Read impiously, this is taken as speaking of the Godhead; read piously, of the saving plan. The subject here is not being made (look: the man did not make the woman), and the order Paul used does not have that in view. It looks only to subordination, not to any difference of nature. In general, what is in view here is not the Godhead of the Only-begotten but the saving plan, which stands closer by nature to the man and the woman.

The followers of Arius say, “As Christ is head of the man because he is his maker, so God is head of Christ as his maker.” They seem not to know what comes next: “the head of the woman is the man.” He is not her maker, and he is of one substance with her; and on the same reasoning we turn out to be of one substance with Christ. So they talk nonsense about everything. “Head” is used here in the sense of ruling, not of making. So whoever has Christ as ruler and head insults his own ruler when he sins. On this reasoning, by being subject to Christ we are subject to God the Father, because God is also the head of Christ.

On 1 Corinthians 11:4: By “prophesying” he means interpreting the prophets. Or else the difference between the prophets of old and the new ones lies here: the old prophets spoke in general terms about the Jews' falling away, the calling of the nations and Christ's coming in the flesh, while the new ones spoke of particular cases, as Peter did with Ananias.

On 1 Corinthians 11:7: From these words it appears that man is the image of God neither in his soul nor in his body. If he were the image in either of these, the woman too would certainly have been called the image of God, since she too has the form of a body and a soul like the man's. If the woman has the same soul and flesh as the man and is still not called the image, then clearly man is the image of God in his rule. When the discussion concerns the creatures without reason, the woman too is the image of God. But when man is weighed against women, the man alone is the image, because male and female among human beings rule over everything on the earth, in the sea and in the air, while the man rules over the woman, and no one on earth rules over the man. As nothing that exists rules over God, so nothing on earth rules over the man. By “nature” we understand the truth of the things themselves.
The second catena form adds: Just as the man who obeys his Sovereign well is the glory and praise of God, so the woman who is rightly subject to him is the glory of the man.

On 1 Corinthians 11:10: The apostle says this because he has seen how rough and unyielding women are, and he reminds them that God has also set angels over us. Some say that the priests of the church are called “angels” here, and that women cover their heads because of them, since women have not been given the freedom to rule. Perhaps he said this because women too used to prophesy by the Holy Spirit. When the Spirit is at work, the ministering angels must be present, and so the woman must cover her head.

On 1 Corinthians 11:14–15: He judged this not by ancient custom but by the custom of their own day. Even those who wore their hair long in the old days cut part of it off, though they wore it longer than they should have; but for a woman to be shorn was always disapproved.
On 1 Corinthians 11:19: By “factions” he means not factions over doctrine but factions over customs and practices.

On 1 Corinthians 11:20–21: He rebukes them because, when they came together as if for communion in the holy body, they did not wait for one another. Some were kept busy by their poverty and came late, and the well-off got in first and did not wait for the others. In their gluttony they neglected the Lord's supper, and toward the…

"the earth and everything that fills it" echoes Psalm 24:1 (LXX 23:1) as cited in 1 Corinthians 10:26; Severianus paraphrases, so no inline citation.

Doublet collapsed: on 11:7 the second form ("Man is the image of God not in body or soul but in rule ... as no one rules over God, so no one over the man on earth") repeats the first and is not printed; its last sentence (the man obeying his Sovereign is God's glory, the woman subject to him the man's glory) is printed under "The second catena form adds:".
